# The Museum of Almost

On her first morning as director, Mara found a wooden boat in the museum’s front hall.

It was twelve feet long, painted blue along one side and bare on the other. A stiff brush rested in a jar beside it. The paint in the jar had hardened around the bristles, preserving the angle at which someone had abandoned the work.

There was no delivery receipt.

“Did we order this?” she asked.

Elias, the caretaker, leaned on his mop.

“We don’t order anything.”

“Then who brought it?”

“Usually that becomes apparent.”

Mara had been hired because she had experience with archives, municipal budgets, and declining attendance. The job description had not mentioned mysterious boats. It had also omitted the smell of wet wool that drifted through the building every afternoon, regardless of weather.

She walked around the boat. On the stern, someone had penciled a name beneath the unfinished paint.

*Margaret.*

Her mother’s name.

***

The Museum of Almost occupied a former post office between a dentist and a shop that sold expensive olive oil. Its limestone façade bore the weathered inscription NEITHER SNOW NOR RAIN, after which the remaining words had been removed during renovations.

Inside were seven galleries of unfinished things.

A wedding dress with one sleeve. A chess game abandoned after the thirty-seventh move. The first nine chapters of a detective novel, accompanied by a sealed envelope containing the author’s intended solution.

Mara had opened the envelope during her interview.

It contained the words: *I hoped I would know by then.*

The previous director, a woman named Dr. Bell, had disappeared in circumstances the trustees described as retirement. Her office contained an umbrella, seventeen years of immaculate expense reports, and a note tucked beneath the telephone.

*Do not accept donations from people who are still angry.*

Mara had assumed this was practical fundraising advice.

Now she suspected it was an operational rule.

She found Elias replacing a lightbulb above an unfinished portrait. The sitter had a finely rendered mouth, one complete ear, and no eyes.

“My father was building that boat,” she said.

“I wondered.”

“He died eleven years ago.”

Elias climbed down.

“Then it’s taken its time.”

***

Her father had started the boat when Mara was fourteen. Every Saturday he went into the garage with a mug of tea, switched on the radio, and worked until lunchtime.

By sixteen she had stopped asking when it would be ready.

By eighteen she had acquired a sharpened opinion about men who started things and did not finish them.

He was a surveyor. He could calculate gradients, settle boundary disputes, and explain why a wall had cracked simply by looking at the ground beneath it. Yet the boat remained stubbornly boat-shaped without becoming a boat.

After his death, her mother sold the house.

Mara assumed the buyers had disposed of it.

Seeing it now, she felt irritation before grief. Even here, even after all this time, it was taking up space.

“Can we send it back?” she asked.

“To where?”

“The garage. Wherever it came from.”

Elias considered the hull.

“You can move it to Gallery Three. There’s room beside the unbuilt railway.”

“That’s a model railway.”

“Most of it.”

***

The municipal inspector arrived on Tuesday.

Her name was Sal Venn, and she carried a tablet in a waterproof case. Rain shone on her shoulders. She declined tea, accepted a chair, and asked Mara to describe the museum’s public purpose.

“We preserve unfinished cultural artifacts.”

Sal typed.

“Why?”

Mara had prepared for questions about accessibility, emergency lighting, and the unreliable boiler.

“Because they offer insight into the creative process.”

“Do they?”

“Among other things.”

Sal looked through the office doorway at a display case containing half a knitted sock.

“My aunt has a room full of that.”

The inspection had been triggered by a ceiling leak. Water had entered Gallery Five and damaged an unfinished map of the city, producing three streets that did not exist.

Mara had not mentioned this in her report.

Sal examined the damp plaster. She examined the visitor figures. She examined a fire exit blocked by the first half of a mechanical elephant.

Then she explained the situation.

The museum needed a new roof, electrical work, and a compelling reason to receive public money.

“You have six weeks,” she said.

“Until what?”

“The committee meeting.”

“And if they say no?”

Sal looked apologetic but not uncertain.

“Then we find another use for the building.”

***

That evening Mara stayed late to read the accession registers.

At first they seemed conventional: dates, descriptions, provenance. Gradually she noticed that the dates did not correspond to manufacture or donation.

The wedding dress had arrived forty years after its maker married someone else.

The mechanical elephant had appeared the morning its inventor’s grandson dismantled his workshop.

A single unposted letter had arrived on a day described simply as *too late*.

In the oldest register, written in brown ink, she found a paragraph explaining the collection.

*An unfinished thing may persist in the world long after the hands that began it have let go. Most are absorbed into ordinary life. Some become burdens. A few require temporary shelter.*

Below this, in another hand:

*Temporary is important.*

Mara checked the first accession number.

A stone arch, begun in 1843.

Still on display.

***

She called an emergency trustees’ meeting. Two trustees attended in person; the third joined from a car and repeatedly disappeared whenever his phone slid off the dashboard.

“We need an exhibition,” Mara said. “Something people will come to see.”

“Famous failures,” suggested the treasurer.

“Celebrity shopping lists,” said the trustee in the car.

Mara proposed inviting the public to bring their own unfinished projects. They could tell their stories, contribute to the archive, recognize themselves in the collection.

The trustees liked that recognition cost little.

Elias, who was changing the batteries in the wall clock, did not look pleased.

Afterward he said, “People will bring things they want to get rid of.”

“Yes. That’s how collecting works.”

“Sometimes.”

“We can’t save the museum without visitors.”

He set the clock to the correct time. It immediately lost four minutes.

“You should ask what we’re saving it for.”

***

The exhibition opened on a Saturday.

By noon, a queue stretched past the olive oil shop.

People brought quilts, applications, pottery, business plans, and a language-learning course still wrapped in plastic. A retired electrician arrived with two-thirds of a harpsichord. A woman carried a box labeled TAXES, which Mara declined on the grounds that the museum could not suspend statutory obligations.

Each donor completed a form.

*What is the object?*

*Why was it begun?*

*Why was it left unfinished?*

The third question caused trouble.

People wrote *lack of time*, then crossed it out.

They wrote *circumstances*.

One man sat for twenty minutes before writing, in small capitals, *I FOUND OUT I DID NOT LIKE DOING IT.*

By closing time, Mara had collected eighty-three objects and enough admissions revenue to cover the boiler repair.

She stood among the donations, exhilarated.

Then she noticed the boat had moved.

Its bow now pointed toward the exit.

***

On Monday, a boy came back for a violin.

He was twelve, perhaps thirteen, with a solemn face and a coat too large for him. His mother had donated the instrument along with an exercise book containing six completed lessons.

“She said I’d regret stopping,” he told Mara.

“Do you?”

“No.”

“Then why do you want it back?”

“Because she keeps saying it’s in a museum now. Like that proves something.”

Mara brought him to the intake room.

The violin lay in its open case. A pale rectangle on the velvet showed where its bow had rested.

“Would you like to finish the lessons someday?”

The boy looked at her with exhausted courtesy.

“No. I like swimming.”

Mara handed him the case.

After he left, she retrieved his mother’s donation form.

Under *Why was it left unfinished?* she had written: *He lost confidence.*

Mara put the form in a drawer rather than the archive. She did not know what to replace the answer with.

***

Over the following week, the museum became difficult.

Doors opened into the wrong galleries. The unfinished railway extended across a corridor overnight. Someone discovered a new chapter in the detective novel, but it consisted entirely of the detective walking through rooms, unable to remember what he was investigating.

The donations would not stay where they were placed.

A half-completed degree application appeared on Mara’s desk every morning.

The harpsichord sounded a single note whenever anyone said *potential*.

Elias placed buckets under fresh leaks.

“Is this because of the exhibition?” Mara asked.

“It’s crowded.”

“We have storage.”

“Not that kind of crowded.”

He took her to Gallery Seven, closed since before she arrived. Beneath dust sheets stood hundreds of objects that had never been catalogued.

“How long have these been here?”

“Some longer than I have.”

“Why weren’t they processed?”

“Dr. Bell thought keeping them safe was enough.”

At the back stood a small wooden chair with three legs. Beside it lay the fourth, shaped and sanded, waiting for someone to attach it.

Mara crouched down. There were screw holes in the seat.

For the first time, she wanted to fetch a screwdriver.

***

Instead, she telephoned her mother.

“Do you remember Dad’s boat?”

“Of course.”

“Why didn’t he finish it?”

Her mother was quiet. Mara could hear plates being stacked.

“I don’t think he wanted to.”

“He worked on it for years.”

“He liked working on it.”

“That’s not the same as wanting a boat.”

“No,” her mother said. “It isn’t.”

Mara sat down.

“He told me we’d take it to the lake.”

“We might have. Though neither of us could swim very well.”

“Why didn’t you say anything?”

“About what?”

“About him never finishing.”

Her mother laughed.

“Darling, on Saturdays I had the house to myself. I could read. Your father had his radio. We were both quite happy.”

Mara looked through her office window at the blue-painted hull.

“I thought you must have been disappointed.”

“I was disappointed he died.”

***

The next morning she found an old photograph tucked beneath a loose floorboard in the boat.

Her father stood in the garage, younger than she remembered him. He held a strip of timber against the hull. His mouth was open, probably explaining something to whoever held the camera.

On the workbench behind him were a sandwich, a newspaper, and a vase containing three daffodils.

She studied the flowers.

In all her memories, the garage had been a place of delay. The photograph suggested that her father had been spending his Saturdays somewhere else entirely.

Elias found her sitting on the floor.

“I’ve been thinking about the museum,” she said.

“Dangerous habit for a director.”

“What happens if we finish something?”

“Depends on the thing.”

“What happens if we take it apart?”

“Same answer.”

“And if we let it go?”

He sat beside her, slowly, with one hand on his knee.

“We used to do more of that.”

***

Mara bought tools with the remaining exhibition budget.

The treasurer objected. Tools were not interpretation materials.

“They will be,” she said.

She moved the intake desk into the front hall and changed the forms.

The new questions were:

*Do you want to continue?*

*Would you like someone else to continue?*

*Are you ready to stop?*

There was also a box marked *I don’t know*, which proved essential.

She invited the donors back.

The retired electrician spent three afternoons examining his harpsichord before deciding to salvage the wood. A local school took it for woodworking lessons.

A woman finished the last six inches of a scarf while talking to a stranger who had come to dismantle a model battleship.

The man who did not like pottery smashed his uneven bowls into pieces for a garden mosaic. He wore safety goggles and looked cheerful.

Not everyone approved.

One visitor accused Mara of destroying evidence.

Another asked whether giving up was now a publicly funded activity.

Sal returned to inspect the roof repairs and found twelve people gathered around the three-legged chair.

“Is this an event?” she asked.

“I’m not sure yet,” Mara said.

***

They attached the fourth leg badly.

The chair wobbled.

A joiner named Ruth removed it, explained the problem, and helped a university student fit it properly. The student had donated an unfinished thesis and was not ready to discuss it.

When the chair stood level, everyone applauded except Ruth, who checked the other joints.

Nothing magical happened.

Then Elias removed its accession tag.

The tag crumbled between his fingers.

Across the room, a locked window swung open. Cool air entered the gallery, carrying the smell of bread from the bakery around the corner.

Mara sat on the chair.

It was uncomfortable.

“Probably needs a cushion,” Ruth said.

***

Three days before the committee meeting, Mara worked on the boat.

She did not attempt to finish it. She cleaned out the dust, removed two rusted nails, and sanded a rough edge where visitors might catch their sleeves.

Inside the hull she placed the photograph, protected beneath glass.

The label took longer.

She threw away a version about deferred dreams. She threw away another about the dignity of labor. Finally she wrote:

*Boat built by Daniel Vale between 1989 and 2006.*

*He worked on it most Saturdays.*

*His family believes he enjoyed himself.*

She invited her mother to see it.

Her mother read the label twice, then climbed into the boat before Mara could stop her.

“He kept biscuits under here,” she said, lifting a small hinged seat.

The compartment was empty except for a pencil and a brass screw.

“Well,” her mother said. “Evidently he finished those.”

***

At the committee meeting, Mara showed photographs of the workshops, visitor figures, and estimates for the roof.

She explained the revised collection policy. Objects would be reviewed rather than preserved indefinitely. Some would remain on display. Others could be completed, returned, repurposed, or respectfully dismantled.

A councilor asked how she intended to measure success.

Mara almost said attendance.

Then she described the boy with the violin.

The councilor looked puzzled.

“So you lost an exhibit.”

“Yes.”

“Deliberately?”

“Yes.”

Sal, seated along the wall, made a note.

The funding passed by one vote.

It was less than Mara had requested. The roof would be repaired in stages, and she would have to submit quarterly reports.

Outside, she called Elias.

“We’re staying open.”

“Good,” he said. “Someone’s brought a bridge.”

“A model?”

There was a pause.

“You’d better come back.”

***

By spring, the museum had fewer exhibits and more chairs.

The railway occupied one room instead of three corridors. Its owner’s great-granddaughter came on Thursdays to work out where it should go.

The detective novel remained unfinished, but visitors could borrow pencils and propose solutions. Most blamed the uncle. There was no uncle in the manuscript.

Mara still had difficult days. Donors argued. Grants were refused. The mechanical elephant required an expensive inspection before anyone would agree to switch it on.

Sometimes she sat in her father’s boat to eat lunch.

She liked the smell of the wood, especially when sunlight warmed the hull. From there she could hear people working in the next gallery: a saw, a dropped spoon, somebody asking for help.

One afternoon, a little girl stopped beside her.

“Does it float?”

“I don’t know.”

“Are you going to find out?”

Mara considered this.

“Maybe not.”

The girl ran her hand along the blue paint.

Then she asked if she could get in.
